h1: Brewing a Mexican-style lager at home with flaked maize
title: Mexican-Style Lager With Flaked Maize | Craft Beer School
desc: A 20 litre Mexican-style lager recipe with flaked maize: the grist, mash, hops and the cold schedule that keeps it crisp.
teaser: Flaked maize is the quiet ingredient behind a crisp Mexican-style lager. Here is how much to use and why it needs no cereal cooker.
standfirst: A Mexican-style lager is pale, dry and light on hops, with a soft grainy sweetness from maize. Flaked maize makes it easy at home because the corn has already been cooked. The hard part is the cold fermentation.
sections: Maize lightens the body without thinning the flavour

Most Mexican-style lagers are built like a pilsner with an adjunct. Pale malt does the heavy lifting and maize replaces part of it. Maize brings fermentable starch with very little protein, so the beer finishes drier and paler than an all-malt lager of the same strength. It also leaves a faint sweet corn note that drinkers read as smoothness.

Target numbers for the style: original gravity 1.044 to 1.050, final gravity 1.008 to 1.010, about 4.5 to 5% ABV and 15 to 22 IBU. Colour stays pale straw, around 2 to 4 SRM. Nothing in that list is extreme, which is why every flaw shows.
Flaked maize skips the cereal cook

Raw maize starch only gelatinises well above normal mash temperature, so commercial breweries boil maize grits in a separate cereal cooker before adding them to the main mash. At home you do not need to. Flaked maize has been steamed and rolled, which gelatinises the starch already. It goes straight into the mash tun with the malt.

The one thing we see go wrong: breakfast cornflakes. They are toasted and usually contain sugar, salt and malt flavouring. Buy flaked maize from a homebrew supplier, or ask a feed or grain merchant for plain steam-rolled maize with nothing added.

For 20 litres into the fermenter at around 72% brewhouse efficiency:

  • 3.4 kg pilsner malt (79%)
  • 0.9 kg flaked maize (21%)
  • Mash at 65 °C for 60 minutes for a dry, fermentable wort
  • Boil 75 minutes with the lid off to drive off DMS from the pilsner malt
  • About 35 g of a 4% alpha noble type hop such as Saaz at 60 minutes for roughly 15 to 18 IBU
  • A small aroma addition of 10 g at 10 minutes if you like it

Keep maize between 15 and 25% of the grist. Below that you barely notice it. Above 30% the beer turns thin and the maize sweetness starts to taste like popcorn. Pilsner malt has more than enough enzymes to convert the maize at these levels.
Cold fermentation is where the beer is made

Pitch a clean lager strain at 10 to 12 °C and hold it there. A dry lager yeast needs two sachets for 20 litres of this gravity; one sachet underpitches and invites sulphur and diacetyl. When gravity is about two thirds of the way down, let the fermenter rise to 16 to 18 °C for two or three days. That diacetyl rest lets the yeast clean up the buttery compound before you chill.

Then drop the beer slowly to 0 to 2 °C and lager for four to six weeks. Our guide to brewing a lager at home covers fridge and controller set-ups for Indian summers. If you cannot hold 10 °C, a clean ale strain at 15 °C gets close, which is the route in our kölsch guide.
Water and carbonation keep it crisp

Soft water suits this beer. If your tap or borewell water is hard, cut it 50:50 with RO or packaged drinking water and add 3 to 4 g of calcium chloride to the 20 litres. Aim for mash pH 5.2 to 5.4. High sulphate makes the small hop charge taste harsh.

Carbonate to about 2.6 volumes of CO2. That is livelier than most ales and it matters here, because the bubbles carry the dryness. Serve at 3 to 5 °C. A lime wedge is a serving habit, not a recipe fix: if the beer needs it to taste fresh, look at oxygen pickup at packaging first.

The commonest faults in this style are DMS (cooked corn or tinned sweetcorn), diacetyl (butter) and sulphur from stressed yeast. All three come from process, not recipe. A weak boil, a warm or small yeast pitch and too short a lagering period cause most of them. Judging which fault you have and tracing it back to the brew day is a skill that improves fastest with a trained palate beside you.
Clarity and freshness decide the first impression

People drink this beer from clear glass or straight from the bottle, often very cold, so haze and stale flavours get noticed fast. Two habits help. First, cold crash hard: a few days at 0 °C drops most of the yeast and chill haze. A dose of gelatin, about 1 g dissolved in 100 mL of warm water per 20 litres, clears the rest within two days.

Second, keep oxygen out at packaging. A pale, lightly hopped lager has nothing to hide oxidation behind. Within a few weeks at Indian room temperature, a carelessly bottled batch picks up a papery, honey-like staleness. Purge kegs with CO2, fill bottles from the bottom with a bottling wand and store the finished beer cold if you can. This style is at its best within two to three months of packaging, so brew a quantity you will finish.
Prove the cold before you buy the maize

Before you buy anything, check that you can hold a fermenter at 10 to 12 °C for two weeks. Put a bucket of water in your fridge or chest freezer with a temperature controller and a probe taped to its side, then watch the readings for three days. If the water holds steady, you are ready to order the maize.
faqs: Can I use cornflakes instead of flaked maize?
No. Breakfast cornflakes contain sugar, salt and malt flavouring and are toasted. Use plain steam-rolled flaked maize.
Do I need a cereal mash for flaked maize?
No. Flaking gelatinises the starch, so flaked maize goes straight into the main mash with the malt.
How much flaked maize should I use?
Between 15 and 25% of the grist. About 0.9 kg in a 4.3 kg grist for 20 litres is a good starting point.
Can I brew it with ale yeast?
Yes, a clean ale strain fermented around 15 °C then cold conditioned gives a close result, though slightly fruitier than a true lager.
